We develop a new algorithm for achieving rotational invariance and sparsity in Principal Component Analysis (PCA). This leads to an optimal solution for the $\ell_1$-norm PCA problem with additional constraints for non-negative entries and unit norm, and helps address issues with existing methods that arise due to rotational ambiguity and component collinearity. Based on this achievement, we demonstrate positive results for selecting the number of principal components in $\ell_1$-norm PCA and for the $\ell_1$-norm version of sparse PCA. Our algorithm involves an iterative application of an operator with characteristics similar to a contraction, which facilitates the application of the Banach fixed point theorem and guarantees linear convergence.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, currently, there is growing interest in utilizing pre-trained language models, which can produce the annotation process more efficient. In this work, we explore BERT's potential in facilitating the semantic annotation of a text dataset with emotion-related content. To achieve this, we developed a simple post-training model leveraging BERT, which we used to evaluate and annotate a dataset. The results showed that BERT's performance was on par with human annotators, and surprisingly, it outperformed them in certain cases. Moreover, we discovered that BERT can be effectively incorporated into an interactive annotation tool, which we found to be comparable to human annotators in assessing the correctness of labeled data. Ultimately, our findings suggest that BERT can be an efficient alternative to human annotators for validating labeled data, and it even has the potential to engage in the annotation process itself.

For robots to effectively navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, they need to be able to construct mental maps of their environment based on the data they gather through sensors. The maps they create should be clear and organized, making it easy for the robot to understand its surroundings and plan its path accordingly. In response to the common issue of mapping uncertainty, researchers have explored the use of probabilistic methods to represent the map, but this can lead to navigation instructions that are too general and less efficient. Our new navigation system, HiTMap, takes a different approach by creating a unique, hierarchical diagram of the environment's topology that directly addresses mapping uncertainty, even if the environment is completely unknown. HiTMap organizes the map into distinct levels of representation, separating the identification of rooms from the determination of their characteristics, such as size and layout. This structured format enables efficient navigation by providing specific instructions based on the data gathered, without relying on probabilistic methods. Furthermore, HiTMap increases efficiency in navigation by reducing the computation required, enabling fast recalibration of the map as new data becomes available. We have tested HiTMap successfully in various unknown environments simulated using Gazebo, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding optimal navigation routes.

One of the most sensitive methods for determining changes in a local magnetic field is through atomic interferometry. While this approach can be very sensitive to acceleration and temperature fluctuations, there's a way to make it even more sensitive to magnetic field changes by positioning atomic beams near superconducting materials that exhibit the Meissner effect. Since atomic interferometry is sensitive to the slight deflections of atomic beams caused by the formation of magnetic vortices in the superconductors, this effect could be used to detect very small changes in a local magnetic field, particularly spatial variations. This approach has the potential to compete with the most sensitive methods for detecting magnetic field changes and could be an straightforward way to monitor changes in a local magnetic field in real-time, making it suitable for integrating with atomic interferometry in sensitive applications such as gravity measurements and testing the equivalence principle.

In this view, the traditional parametric mixture model is reinterpreted through the lens of a Dirac measure within the framework of measure-valued fractals. We demonstrate that mixing measures that result in distinct components can be represented by a single measure that incorporates all possible combinations, thereby connecting to the measure-theoretic formulation of the isoperimetric problem. This connection in turn leads to the application of the Krein-Rutman theorem in its general form, where the measure underlying the mixture model can be seen as a fixed point of a mapping associated with the isoperimetric problem, and whose differentiating properties are reflected in the structure of the measure itself.

Due to the complex nature of memory management, developers rarely work directly with memory on GPUs, instead utilizing object-based programming models that simplify memory management at the cost of reduced efficiency. Despite this reduction, object-based programming continues to gain popularity because of its ability to enable efficient and parallel code through simple memory management. However, current object-based programming tools on GPUs are often inefficient in memory usage and slow in performance, and thus, there is a need for a more effective solution. In response to these limitations, we present DynaSOAr, a high-performance, parallel memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs with fast memory allocation and deallocation. DynaSOAr utilizes both hardware and software features to enhance memory management, including a block-based memory layout that optimizes memory usage and a pool-based allocator that accelerates allocation and deallocation through parallelization. Moreover, DynaSOAr includes a simple and efficient fragmentation reduction mechanism to minimize memory waste. By leveraging CUDA and presenting a publicly accessible API, DynaSOAr enables developers to easily integrate the allocator into their existing applications with minimal modification. In our evaluations, DynaSOAr outperforms the current state-of-the-art allocator, including the popular $CUBIN$ allocator, across various benchmarks and real-world applications, demonstrating its potential for widespread use.

We have developed a theoretical framework based on relativistic first principles, taking into consideration spin-orbit interaction and orbital and spin polarization of the adatom and host material. This approach allows for the calculation of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in two-dimensional systems using the exact solution of the Bogoliubov--de Gennes equations. Our method has been applied to the investigation of YSR states in superconducting niobium, focused on the effects of magnetocrystalline anisotropy and spin polarization of the adatom and niobium surface sites. Our findings include the presence of two-dimensional YSR states in the gap of niobium, located at the adatom or cluster sites, as well as pairs of one-dimensional YSR states along the edge of the Brillouin zone. Our calculations have been conducted for both a manganese adatom and a manganese dimer on the niobium (110) surface. Our data demonstrate the presence of spin polarization and magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the binding energy and localization of the YSR states, affecting their distribution and polarization. Our results include the projection of the density of states and distribution of superconducting order parameter within the YSR states, along with the orientation of the spin density and localization of the YSR states across the niobium surface. Our theoretical analysis has been compared to recent scanning tunneling microscopy measurements, providing an explanation for the observed phenomena.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years based on spectral characteristics and rotational velocity. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. A fourth smaller planet with an orbital period of $84.839$ days was also identified, and it's suspected to be an Earth-sized planet. Evaluating the irradiation levels suggests that the innermost planet might reside in the habitable zone, making it a potentially interesting subject for further study.

We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defect states within the rutile TiO2 matrix using a (101) [001] slab model. Both B and N atoms can form covalent bonds with oxygen atoms at the surface, while only N atoms can form bonds with titanium atoms beneath the surface. The distance between the defect atom and the nearby Ti atom affects the binding energy. No magnetic moment is observed for both B and C atoms unless they form bonds with Ti atoms, resulting in a 1$\mu_B$ magnetic moment. The depth of the defect atoms also influences the magnetic moment, with a notable increase when the atom is placed in a hollow site within the (101) surface. The band structures show that the up and down spins exhibit a 0.3 eV energy gap when the defect atoms are located in a hollow site. The magnetic moment diminishes when the slab model is expanded to a (3$\times$1) surface, but it persists in a (2$\times$1) surface corresponding to a 2$\times$1 TiO2(101) surface. Notably, this corresponds to the observed magnetism in natural TiO2(101) surfaces.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin introduced the concept of upper richness within Ramsey theory, specifically focusing on upper bounded graphs. They established that for any given positive integers $k$, $n$, and $r$, there exists a specific large enough graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, denoting its subgraphs as $R(n, r)$, such that any function that maps $k$ vertices to subgraphs of $G$ will result in a subgraph of $G$ that contains at least $k$ copies of $R(n, r)$, is not possible. We investigate upper bounded graphs within infinite, countable graph factors and determine that for any given positive integers $k$ and $r$, there exists a function that maps vertices to subgraphs of $G$ will result in an infinite factor that contains infinitely many copies of $R(n, r)$, is possible, thereby extending Erdos and Galvin's result from 1993.

Our analysis highlights that noise from qudit manufacturing and coupling has different effects on quantum gate operations, specifically how noise related to qudit size affects slope and curvature in the accumulation of errors, and how noise from coupling qudit units influences the accumulation of errors, particularly in simulated Quantum Electrodynamics (sQED). Based on these observations, we can optimize qudit size and gate implementation to reduce error accumulation. Utilizing four-level qudits (quartics or quartits) instead of two-level qudits (qubits) often results in a noise reduction benefit, which we call noise enhancement. The threshold at which qudit size offers a noise reduction benefit varies depending on gate implementation and noise type but can range from 64 to 256 qudit units. Quanterra's qudit manufacturing produces qudit units with a small size offering significant noise reductions (up to 31x) in simulated Quantum Electrodynamics (sQED) while Thorlabs' qudit manufacturing produces qudit units with larger size offering more modest noise reductions (up to 5x). The optimal qudit size also depends on the target quantity being simulated, with larger qudit sizes beneficial for calculating energy spectra than density matrices. The noise reduction benefit (qudit size) increases over time for a fixed qudit unit, indicating that qudit units with a larger size remain stable for longer time periods during the simulation. The data presented can be applied to other quantum simulations that involve qudit units

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of a circularly polarized laser on a thin polarized film target. The results show that even when the intensity of the laser is low compared to its maximum possible intensity, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization, particularly when the orientation of polarization is set to 90 degrees relative to the film target. In such a case, the polarization of the positrons reaches over 20% in a narrow window of light-intensity values. The degree of polarization can be further increased, up to 60%, if the film target is modified to accommodate a larger number of charged particles. The production of dense, polarized positrons at these levels could be achievable with the high-power lasers and small targets that are currently available, offering a potential breakthrough for various applications, including medical research.

Given a finite group G and a subgroup H of G, we examine the structure of H within the group G, focusing on the number of coset types relative to H as our main measure. This count is reflected in our analysis under the label |X_H|, which captures the essence of H's embedding within G. By exploring |X_H|^d, we aim to uncover a meaningful connection to G's underlying properties, specifically its group-theoretical characteristics. Our investigation yields several notable outcomes, including a characterization of G as a 2-group whenever |X_H|^d is minimal and equals 16 for all subgroups H. Furthermore, we establish a connection between |X_H|^d and the group's probability distributions, which can be utilized to identify a subset of G consisting of elements with a specified property, in this case, being abelian.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature detector with a small number of external components. The detector employs two bandgap voltage generators working at different temperatures to provide two distinct voltage outputs, which are then converted into a single temperature-dependent signal. The resulting temperature estimate is obtained by calculating the difference between a reference voltage and a weighted average of the two output voltages. The detector's operation is compatible with both low-voltage and high-temperature applications. The proposed design achieves a temperature range of -25°C to 85°C, offers a precision of 0.24°C, and has an estimated power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion. The proposed design can be integrated into systems that require precise temperature monitoring, including memory, microprocessors, and phase-locked loops.

This study focuses on integrating geometric frameworks from symplectic geometry within the context of Lie groupoids and differential stacks. We demonstrate how the concept of moment maps is refined to accommodate Lie groupoids, and establish the principles of classical mechanics and Hamiltonian group actions are smoothly extended to this environment.

A statistical analysis of infrared dark clouds was used to develop a framework for identifying core evolution, specifically the stage preceding massive star formation. By comparing the mass and radius of 19 gas-filled cores within the Dragon infrared cloud using radiative transfer modeling, the authors found that, on average, precursors with higher mass ranges have greater density and smaller radii. This trend is attributed to self-gravity, and the authors suggest that pressure may also play a significant role. The distribution of densities and radii from both theoretical models and observations show a clear distinction, indicating that in many cases, dense cores are not completely embedded within a surrounding, less dense envelope. The authors further propose that core expansion could be a critical factor in massive star formation, and they suggest evaluating this idea with accurate measurements of core velocities and radii.

We develop a one-step recurrence formula to represent Gaussian random fields on the sphere at a single point in time, building on the work of Papadopoulos et al. (2020) which described a two-step recurrence. This formula has useful applications in fields such as remote sensing and astronomy that involve the analysis of spherical random signals over time.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface properties, especially when they have a high interfacial tension relative to their bulk properties.  Despite the significance of this phenomenon in natural and engineering contexts, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.  This study delves into the relationship between surface characteristics and friction in liquid foams, demonstrating that irregular surface textures can substantially increase friction even when the total surface area remains constant.  This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in foams with high air pressures, where the frictional force is directly proportional to the curvature of the surface texture.  A simple theoretical model also explains the effects of surface texture on frictional forces in liquid foams, highlighting the critical influence of the contact angle and surface curvature in this context.

This report details our methods that led to 2nd and 3rd place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 of CHU-2022, a skin cancer classification challenge organized by the University of Bahrain. To address the issues identified in the previous report, we implemented additional quality control measures for our training data. This was achieved by introducing the Shannon entropy of the dermatologist's diagnosis, aiming to focus on patients with a clear diagnosis. We also developed a robust approach to handle outlier samples outside the scope of our model. This was done by creating separate networks for rejection, similar to the approach described in [8].

The interaction between a rapidly spinning inner cylinder and a surrounding fluid, which occupies a rectangular Hele-Shaw cell, can be compromised by the introduction of an opposing fluid with significantly distinct properties. This opposing fluid can originate from within the cell or be introduced through its side walls. The rotation's effectiveness in preventing the interface from becoming unstable depends on various factors, including the speed of rotation, the difference in fluid properties and the shape of the cell. The conservation of mass and momentum in a frame of reference that is relative to the spinning cylinder have been used to develop a mathematical model that describes the resulting pattern of interface instability. This model has been applied to different scenarios of fluid interaction and provides a comparative analysis of the resulting patterns of instability. It has been observed that even slight irregularities in the cell's walls can contribute to the interface's instability and that the direction of the resulting pattern is determined by the orientation of the cell. The effectiveness of rotation in preventing interface instability can vary, even when the cell's shape remains constant, due to changes in the interface's curvature. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene and 2-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. Additionally, a lack of detection is reported for 1-propynyl-1-cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH2) at a column density threshold of 0.02 times that of cyclopentadiene. The calculated abundances of these ethynyl and cyano cyclopentadiene isomers or variants suggest they may form through neutral-neutral reactions, and the detection of ethynyl cyclopentadiene is confirmed to be roughly twice as abundant as cyanocyclopentadiene (CCH versus CN variants).

In neural machine translation, the focus method selects specific neurons to limit the translation output based on input meanings, but it doesn't consider the importance of neurons in the output vocabulary. To address this, we propose a novel look-ahead focus method that initially weighs the output vocabulary neurons and then uses the weighted sequence as input for the next translation generation. Unlike existing focus methods, our approach doesn't require a separate training process and can be seamlessly integrated into existing sequence-to-sequence translaters. We evaluate our proposed method on four machine translation datasets and find it outperforms the baseline focal translator in terms of translation quality.

The significant progress achieved in grid computing was not merely the result of cumulative efforts, but was also greatly facilitated by a well-structured framework. A project, dubbed the Translating Grid Project, played a crucial role in streamlining grid computing development by introducing a unifying framework consisting of interchangeable layers. Although the project's impact on grid computing has been evident, its underlying principles and contributions to grid computing have received only limited attention in the scientific community. This paper seeks to explore the Translating Grid Project's conceptual foundation, investigate its effect on grid computing, and examine what lessons can be learned from its successful implementation.

A novel model, called the Dissipative Unified Dark Substance (DUDES) model, is presented for
examining the interplay between dark matter and dark energy. This model incorporates an
invariant cosmological term within the Einstein field equations, which are then expanded to
include gradients of the metric components and relativistic bulk velocities of matter and
radiation. The DUDES model encompasses various dark matter and dark energy scenarios,
such as $f(R)$ theories, scalar fields, fractional powers in the Hubble parameter, and an
invasive cosmological constant. The model's parameters were determined through a data-
driven analysis utilizing a modified version of the $f(R)$ theory, which demonstrated an
accurate fit to observational data, specifically with regards to the Hubble constant, the
cosmological constant, and the overall expansion history of the universe. However, during
this analysis, an abnormal decrease in the Hubble constant at higher redshifts was observed.

This study explores the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting a likelihood fit to lattice QCD predictions and theoretical neutrino operator analyses. This analysis led to constraints on neutrino properties and the dark matter operator, which were then compared to existing limits. Furthermore, we established lower bounds on neutrino mass eigenvalues, determined the visibility of dark matter at various J/ψ rates, and explored the potential for future experiments to detect dark matter at facilities like the Brookhaven Generic TPC or the J-PET scanner.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The local time $L_t(x)$ of a random walk $S_t$ is defined as the number of times the walk $S_t$ has visited the point $x$ up to time $t$. We prove that for a one-dimensional simple random walk $S_t$ with discrete time, the process $L_t$ will likely spend its time at a particular value of $x$ for an extended period of time, despite not being a stationary process. More specifically, for any small $\epsilon>0$, the probability that the random walk stays within $\epsilon$ units of its most visited site for an extended period of time, on the order of $\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\epsilon)$, finally exceeds a certain threshold is very low.

A plasma source called IShTAR has been developed for testing plasma interactions in the context of a neutralizer that will be used for Mars sampling return mission. To ensure accurate testing, it's crucial to understand how plasma affects the neutralizer's performance and component longevity. Therefore, a precise characterization of IShTAR's plasma is necessary. A study was conducted to validate the plasma source's functionality in helicon mode, as specified in the design requirements. The study found that IShTAR's plasma source can operate in helicon mode, producing plasma with the desired characteristics. Specifically, it generates 1.5 times the expected plasma density and 10% lower plasma flux than the designed specifications. Additionally, reducing the plasma source's power from 10.5 to 5.5 kilowatts resulted in a decrease in plasma density but had a minimal impact on plasma flux. This validation is a crucial step in using IShTAR for testing the neutralizer's performance under various plasma conditions.

While gold-standard nuclear manual segmentation from histology images remains the gold standard for cancer diagnosis, reducing annotation time without sacrificing accuracy is crucial for developing real-world cancer diagnosis systems. To achieve this, a novel approach called W-Net has been presented, which applies two consecutive convolutional networks to achieve accurate and efficient nuclear segmentation. Firstly, a lightweight convolutional network called P-Net quickly identifies and outlines individual nuclei by creating a map of probability values representing likely nucleus locations. Subsequently, a second network called D-Net refines the results from P-Net by eliminating any residual errors through a subtractive strategy, thereby further enhancing the accuracy of nucleus segmentation. The framework's efficiency is attributed to W-Net's ability to derive optimal weights for P-Net and D-Net collectively, allowing for seamless learning of the desired representation learning capabilities. Experimental evaluations conducted on two separate datasets have demonstrated the superiority of W-Net over existing manual segmentation methods, showcasing a notable 78% reduction in annotation time without compromising segmentation accuracy.

Let's consider a non-abelian group G that acts on a set X in a locally finite manner and incorporate the action of G into the permutation representation acting on the set X. We then define the algebra associated with this action as the quotient of the group algebra by the ideal consisting of elements with zero support. It is known that in characteristic zero, the exchange theorem holds for this algebra with respect to a specific subalgebra when certain conditions are met. This paper expands on this concept by demonstrating the validity of the exchange theorem in characteristic p (for p greater than 2) for specific subalgebras within the permutation representation associated with the action of G on X.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then depicted as non-linear differential equations. The soliton and black hole solutions are examined to determine their stability and temperature, with calculations showing that the soliton solutions are stable for all possible symmetry groups, while black hole solutions exist only for the $so(3,1)$ group. The soliton solutions can also exist in the $so(3,1)$ group, but are unstable. The holographic entropy for both the black hole and soliton solutions can be calculated, along with the holographic energy for the soliton solutions. The stability of gauge fields for both solutions can be analyzed, along with calculations showing that all possible gauge fields can exist as multipoles in the soliton solutions, whereas in the black hole solutions only the monopole gauge field can exist.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Despite its advantages, the medical application of elastography is limited due to poor image quality resulting from inadequate tissue sampling, especially in ultrasound elastography. Developing accurate models to predict the behavior of tissues under external pressure can significantly enhance the imaging capability of elastography. Unfortunately, models based on partial differential equations require laborious computation and are often infeasible for real-time imaging. In contrast, the proposed Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method leverages the distinctive source sampling pattern of elastography without relying on partial differential equations, by reconstructing images based on synthetic aperture techniques. Simulation results under realistic conditions demonstrate the VSSA approach to be a practical and efficient solution for estimating the physical properties of tissues, enabling accurate estimation even with a small sampling footprint of 3x3, and showing significant performance enhancements over conventional synthetic aperture techniques.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the $k$-centers clustering problem, we divide data points into clusters based on their proximity to predetermined center points. This problem has various applications, particularly in identifying representative points for large datasets. Given a set $P$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we seek to find the minimum number of centers, $k$, required to create clusters that include all points and have a maximum diameter of $D$. This problem stands out from traditional clustering problems because it determines the optimal number of centers solely based on the input points' dimensions, without considering their distribution. In this research, we develop a approximately linear-time algorithm that approximately solves the problem within a factor of $O(\log n)$ for any number of centers and in $\mathbb{R}^d$ dimensions. Specifically, for a given number of centers $k$, our algorithm yields a solution with a diameter of $O(\log n)\times (D+\sqrt{d\cdot \sigma_P^2})$ and includes all points in the resulting clusters. Here, $\sigma_P$ denotes the Gaussian standard deviation of the point set $P$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games are first solved on a coarser state-based representation, which are then combined into a comprehensive'metagame' that accounts for all interactions between the scaled-down state categories. Each of these scaled games can be resolved through various existing methods, allowing our framework to leverage multiple hierarchical strategies. By aggregating the set of scaled games, we create a compact representation that efficiently enables efficient exploration and learning of the original large-scale game. A novel algorithm is provided for constructing the metagame, as well as multiple ways to integrate the aggregated states into the original game. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our hierarchical approach, showcasing significant performance gains over multiple existing methods.

While the number of forward-going neutrons in neutron-rich matter can be computed with the Boltzmann-Vlasov equation, due to the large disparity between the strong interaction range (approximately 1 fm) and the length scale of neutron probes (farther than 100 fm) a new "Vector Boson Approximation in the Finitely Extended Source" model is needed. This new model considers the finite extent of sources and accurately accounts for the interference between the strong interaction and extendence effects. It is particularly effective at predicting the behavior of vector mesons like $\rho$, $\eta$/$\eta'$, $a_0$, $b_1$, and $f_2(1275)$ in laboratory energies from 1 to 10 GeV, a range achievable in experiments using a muon collider or the J-PET detector.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to serious degradation when tasks are highly distinct.
We attribute this unfavorable outcome to catastrophic interference among the
tasks. To overcome this interference, we propose two approaches: changing the
way tasks are represented and using separate components of the model to reduce
sharing. Both strategies are effective in preventing the decline in performance
and help us confirm that the drop in performance is indeed a result of
interference. Our proposed methods also outperform other compared methods on a
wide range of multi-task environments.

We explore an interesting development where Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem leads to an unforeseen consequence - the undecidability of arithmetic within certain formal systems. To demonstrate this, we establish a connection between the incompleteness theorem and the decidability of arithmetic, showing they are equivalent in certain contexts. E.Sh. Livshits initially suggested this connection in 1956, and we examine its background and implications. Notably, the equivalence implies that if we have a formal system that includes arithmetic and is capable of making certain specific logical statements, then that system must be inherently incomplete and undecidable. One such example is a well-known formal system from 1931 proposed by Kurt Godel, Godel's beta-function arithmetic. Another example is a formal system from 1931 proposed by Alonzo Church, known as lambda calculus, which also exhibits both incompleteness and undecidability.

We investigate the function $f\in NV$ within Clifford analysis, where $NV$ denotes the space of functions devoid of zeros and singularities. The purpose of this study is to examine the behavior of $f$ in relation to its eigenfunctions in three-dimensional space. By applying the Cauchy-type problem for the Dirac operator, we establish the presence of three distinct balls, one containing the singular region, one enclosing the zero region, and a third enclosing both, such that $f$ exhibits no zeros or singularities within this third ball.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on minimizing the difference between the restored and true images, but also on selecting the most likely one. This phenomenon is reflected in a Bayesian framework with multiple modes rather than a single minimum, which makes traditional optimization-based methods less effective. In contrast, deep learning-based methods can handle multiple modes more effectively, but often produce low-quality images due to mode collapse, leading to less accurate restorations. We present a new framework, called RCGAN, that prevents mode collapse by adding multiple normal penalties to the objective function of a deep conditional GAN, resulting in a regularized formulation that can be solved as a dual problem. We also derive a theorem to analyze the relationship between the normal penalties, the quality of restorations, and the prior distribution, which enables the implementation of appropriate regularization strategies based on statistical properties of the prior distribution. We conduct extensive experiments on various imaging tasks, including MRI with multiple scans, single-pixel compressive imaging, and image deblurring, and show that RCGAN outperforms other deep learning-based references in terms of both subjective and objective quality.

This article examines the existence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. A key requirement for surfaces to be invariant involves the Lie derivative of the surface's equation being equal to zero. This process is applied to a specific surface in a dynamical system defined by the equation $\dot{x} = \alpha(t) f(x)$, where $x$ represents the surface, $f(x)$ represents the vector field, and $\alpha(t)$ is a scalar function. To determine conditions under which surfaces are invariant, we establish a relationship between the index of the vector field $f(x)$ and the scalar function $\alpha(t)$, drawing on the properties of the vector field's index which arises in the context of singularities in dynamical systems. This analysis is initially developed for systems in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and then generalized to systems in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

The interstellar medium is capable of complex and remote analysis through the use of pulsar scintillation patterns. This study delves into the detailed analysis of pulsar B1133+16's scintillation, facilitated by its exceptionally bright signal enabling the high-resolution observation of small-scale scintillation patterns. Utilizing data collected by the LWA1 telescope during a two-year period, researchers identified multiple stations of scintillation patterns at pulsar B1133+16's beam, specifically in the direction of the 3 kpc spherical shell and the faint scintillation patterns within the solar neighborhood. Furthermore, the observation of both small-scale scintillation patterns and the associated phase shifts at various frequencies allows for the accurate measurement of the line-of-sight electron density within a few parsecs from the Earth. This technique also revealed a declining density of about 0.05 $e^{-20}\pc^{-1}$ in the line-of-sight electron density in the solar neighborhood.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through extended convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked convolution neural networks, but the lack of control over frequency output limitations its practical applications. To address this challenge, we introduce a new expanded convolution neural network with variable kernel sizes, allowing for efficient pitch-dependent signal processing. In QPNet, pitch-dependent extended convolutions are used in place of traditional convolutions, resulting in a large number of parameters. To tackle this challenge, we apply quantization and expand convolution techniques, incorporating previous acoustic features to reduce the parameter size. The evaluation of QPNet on the LJSpeech dataset demonstrates comparable quality to WaveNet and VQ-VAE-TD-P, as well as superior mean opinion score (MOS) scores for pitch and voice. Moreover, QPNet exhibits notable entropy reduction values for both pitch and voice, indicating its effectiveness in capturing complex phenomena with low entropy. The simple and efficient method of training QPNet enables the generation of high-quality audio with relatively small model sizes, making it a cost-effective solution for real-world applications.

Bicategories incorporate bicategory morphisms as objects, providing a higher-category framework that encompasses the principles of marked categories in a more comprehensive format. Building on the concept of shadows introduced by Leinster, this paper demonstrates that bicategories are essentially defined by bicategory morphisms and shadows applied to bicategory morphisms. A detailed analysis follows, illustrating the relationship between shadows and bicategories through the example of functor pairs.

Deep neural networks rely on robust training data, and certain distorted images can significantly hinder training. Researchers have investigated methods for finding the most challenging noise patterns that severely impair a deep neural network's performance, an optimization problem known as the "hardest sphere" problem. We show that one common approach to estimating the most difficult noise pattern, centered on a specific feature, involves overestimating the pattern's size. Our analysis provides a precise lower bound for this pattern's radius and suggests an efficient algorithm for finding a near-optimal solution to the hardest sphere problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in multiple benchmark datasets and applications, including outperforming existing competing methods according to a key evaluation criterion.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the massive amount of data being generated and the importance of scaling graph-based models. Unfortunately, many current GNN techniques rely on fast-computing integer distances on graphs, which hinders their performance when dealing with large datasets. This paper introduces a novel neural network called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN) that calculates operations using the Lorentzian distance, allowing for learning from data without being limited by large input sizes. LGNN maintains flexible connectivity without being constrained by Euclidean similarity constraints, making it particularly suitable for modeling complex relationships and combinations of features. Experimental results show that LGNN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art GNNs across 6 different classification tasks, demonstrating the benefits of Lorentzian learning.

This research focuses on identifying an object within a wave equation that represents the interaction between a structural and acoustic system, using measurements from the acoustic system alone. A solution to this problem is referred to as a qualitative unique recovery, indicating that the object in question is consistently determined by these measurements. For a non-empty boundary condition and a specific type of wave equation, we provide qualitative unique recovery results. Additionally, we offer a novel approach to solving a related quantitative unique recovery problem. A key aspect of our strategy involves converting the original problem into an optimal control problem, achieving a level of accuracy in our solution by adjusting the parameters of the control problem.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

In this note, we explore a specific class of gravity theories, known as "hefty gravity", which are defined by a unique property of their perturbation theories. Within this framework, we examine the concept of harmonic gauge and discuss its multiple interpretations. Specifically, we show that in plenty of cases, the harmonic gauge corresponds to multiple choices, rather than a singular one. Furthermore, we connect this finding to a recent result involving the consistency of hefty gravity in a certain low-energy regime.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, thereby illustrating the underlying classical mathematical structure of this representation. This transformation exposes the representation's intrinsic symplectic structure and identifies the condition for temperate Hamiltonians, thereby providing a more straightforward proof of the positivity of the operator-valued integral. Additionally, this approach yields a straightforward proof of the inverse of the Fourier transform that maps from the Heisenberg Lie algebra to its dual.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the easiest $s$-channel susy model, we examine the consistency of electroweak symmetry breaking and determine the parameter region that allows for the extrapolation of dark matter scattering cross-section off nucleons, while also assessing the reliability of Higgs vacuum stability predictions. By confronting leading log perturbative and numerical results, we identified a limited region of parameters where the likelihood for vacuum instability is considered low, specifically within the easiest $s$-channel susy model's simplest variant. Here, we find that the preferred region for minimal flavor violation shows a unique pattern when constrained by the leading log approach. Furthermore, this model reveals connections between dark matter phenomenology, neutrino characteristics, and the ease with which the easiest $s$-channel susy model's simplest variant can be tested at LHC and future monopole searches.

We employ group theory and orbital degeneracy elimination to investigate the level crossing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ energy levels in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with octahedral crystal fields. By analyzing the point group symmetry of these materials, specifically focusing on the effect of slight distortions from $O_h$, we map the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ energy levels in 6d transition metal oxides are mapped for the first time. Our results show that in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides small perturbations from $O_h$ symmetry can break the degeneracy of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals, leading to level splitting. We outline the possible level crossings in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with $O_h$ symmetry and also identify the magnetic properties of these materials.

This research focuses on the relative quantum Chern-Simons invariant, a theoretical concept within the realm of geometric topology. We demonstrate that this invariant remains unchanged under a specific type of geometric transformations known as birational transformations, which maintain the underlying mathematical structure despite potentially altering the representation of the associated algebraic variables. This consistency holds true for a broad range of complex mathematical constructs, including noncompact configurations and those based on algebraic surfaces with fundamental properties, as long as they possess certain essential characteristics that ensure validity.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging is being explored that involves incorporating realistic symptoms of lung diseases into artificially created images. This innovative use case builds on existing GAN-based techniques for manipulating medical images but diverges from their standard approach, which focuses on training models to distinguish real images from generated ones. In contrast, this research configures the discriminator as a traditional multi-class classifier, surpassing the existing record for accurately identifying 14 classes of abnormal chest X-rays, from 72.1% according to the CheX128 dataset to 76.3%. Additionally, an experimental feature is demonstrated that involves edifying a model to incorporate specific abnormalities into generated images, demonstrating its potential in realistic image editing by combining images and accounting for biases in the dataset.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool enables users to easily visualize high-dimensional data through embedding techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and others, and to interact with these visualizations for cluster and anomaly identification. With features like dynamic visualization of high-dimensional data, ViDaExpert facilitates a deeper understanding of multivariate interactions and patterns of data.
